text: MySQL has its own family of functions that look similar to T-SQL's, but are spelled differently or behave a little differently. Start with NULL-coalescing: T-SQL's two-argument ISNULL becomes MySQL's IFNULL — same idea, same two arguments, different name. Both platforms also support the standard COALESCE, which takes any number of arguments and is the more portable choice when you need more than two candidates.

Next, string aggregation across grouped rows. T-SQL's STRING_AGG takes the separator as a second, comma-separated argument. MySQL's GROUP_CONCAT puts the separator keyword INSIDE the function call instead — GROUP_CONCAT product name SEPARATOR comma-space. Small syntax difference, but a real one, and if you forget the SEPARATOR keyword MySQL just defaults to a bare comma.

You already met this one back in Chapter Three: MySQL quotes identifiers that clash with reserved words using backticks, where T-SQL uses square brackets. Backtick order, backtick group, backtick settings — same job, different punctuation.

And finally, a genuine historical quirk: MySQL has traditionally been more lenient than T-SQL, Oracle, or PostgreSQL about comparing mismatched types. Comparing product_id, a number column, against the string '5' — in quotes — has historically just worked in MySQL, silently coercing the string into a number.

This connects directly back to sql_mode from two lessons ago: stricter modes tighten up some of this implicit coercion, pulling MySQL's behavior closer to what you're used to elsewhere. But regardless of which mode a given server happens to be running, explicit CAST or CONVERT is always the safer habit.

IFNULL instead of ISNULL, GROUP_CONCAT with an inline SEPARATOR instead of STRING_AGG's second argument, backticks instead of brackets, and a historically looser attitude toward type mixing. Next lesson: storage engines, and why the one your table happens to use is actually a developer's problem, not just a DBA's. See you there.
